solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Grace’s headdress Ruth completely defaced? (8)

indicatorNotes.completely defaced: both words lose their faces, i.e. their first letters

blocks.note: TURBAN with its first letter removed
ruth is an old word for PITY; PITY without its first letter

annotation.surface: Someone called Ruth has vandalised the headscarf of a woman called Grace.
annotation.walkthrough: Grace and Ruth read as two women's names; Grace is the definition (polished manners) and ruth is the old noun for pity, as in ruthless. 'Completely' makes both words lose their heads.
annotation.definitionFit: Urbanity is suave, refined courtesy, which is one sense of grace.

entries.clue: Addict’s bum steer ignored every so often (4)

indicatorNotes.ignored every so often: letters are dropped at regular intervals, leaving the even ones

annotation.surface: An addict keeps being given bad advice and sometimes ignores it.
annotation.walkthrough: A bum steer is a piece of misleading advice; here it is only a string of letters. The odd letters B, M, T, E go and the even ones stay.
annotation.definitionFit: Drug slang: someone who uses regularly is a user, the everyday word for an addict.

entries.clue: Consumer guidance from road-test — beef with BSE condemned (4-6,5)

indicatorNotes.condemned: condemned things are torn down, so the letters are wrecked and rebuilt

blocks.note: anagram fodder; BSE is mad cow disease

annotation.surface: A food test finds beef infected with mad cow disease, and consumers are warned.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole surface is a food-safety scare, so 'condemned' reads as meat being declared unfit rather than as an instruction to rearrange the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Best-before dates on packaging guide shoppers on how long food keeps.

entries.clue: Currently, negative votes over mass cuts (8)

indicatorNotes.cuts: the pieces cut into, i.e. go inside, NAYS

blocks.note: nays are votes against; split as N...AYS
O = over, as in cricket scores
a wad is a mass or lump

annotation.surface: A mass of no votes is now forcing cuts.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a vote against spending cuts, but 'cuts' is the container instruction: the over-plus-mass pair cuts into the negative votes.
annotation.definitionFit: Nowadays means at the present time, currently.

entries.clue: One who takes unlimited throws in paper round (5)

indicatorNotes.unlimited: without its limits, i.e. first and last letters
indicatorNotes.in: the trimmed word goes inside the paper
indicatorNotes.round: the paper goes round the trimmed word

blocks.note: FT = the Financial Times, split around the insert
SHIES (throws, as at a coconut shy) without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A paper boy on his round keeps flinging papers without restraint.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a paper round; 'round' here tells FT to go round the trimmed word, and 'unlimited' means shorn of both end letters, not boundless.
annotation.definitionFit: A thief is someone who takes what is not theirs.

entries.clue: English queen and king pressed by conceited young man in rally (4,2)

indicatorNotes.pressed by: squeezed on both sides by the outer word

blocks.note: a pup is an arrogant young man

annotation.surface: An arrogant youth pushes forward at a rally to get close to the English royals.
annotation.walkthrough: Rally reads as a gathering but is the verb meaning to recover. A pup is a cheeky or conceited young man, dated British usage.
annotation.definitionFit: To perk up is to rally, to recover spirits or health.

entries.clue: Fake fivers a Tzigane checks (6)

indicatorNotes.checks: holds back, restrains, so the words contain the answer

blocks.note: runs from the fourth letter of the first word into the start of the last

annotation.surface: A Hungarian Gypsy inspects banknotes to see if they are counterfeit.
annotation.walkthrough: Checks reads as inspects; it is 'restrains', the letters held inside. A fiver is a five-pound note and a Tzigane is a Hungarian Gypsy.
annotation.definitionFit: Ersatz means imitation or substitute, a fake.

entries.clue: Blow joint cash in weekend on vacation abroad (7,8)

indicatorNotes.on vacation: the word is vacated, emptied of its middle

blocks.note: the knuckle is a finger joint
WEEKEND with its middle letters removed

annotation.surface: Someone smokes a joint, blows their money and cashes in on a weekend holiday abroad.
annotation.walkthrough: Blow and joint point to drugs and 'on vacation abroad' to a holiday; the drugs picture is a decoy. A knuckle sandwich is slang for a punch in the mouth.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang: a fist delivered to the mouth, knuckles served up like a snack, is a punch or blow.

entries.clue: Suitors showing clear disputes (10)

annotation.surface: Rival lovers make their quarrels obvious.
annotation.walkthrough: Suitors suggests wooers, but here it means people who bring a suit in court.
annotation.definitionFit: Plaintiffs bring lawsuits, so they are suitors in the legal sense.

entries.clue: American spin mostly defends eg circumstantially awarded degree? (8)

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of the word but not all of it, so its last letter is lost

annotation.walkthrough: An aegrotat (Latin 'he is ill') is a degree granted to a student too ill to sit the exams, hence 'circumstantially' and the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: An aegrotat is awarded on account of circumstances (illness) rather than exam performance.

entries.clue: Former Welsh international regularly turned out (9)

indicatorNotes.regularly: take letters at regular intervals: the odd ones
indicatorNotes.out: the letters are put out of order

annotation.surface: A former Wales player used to turn out for the side regularly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned out' reads as played for a team, and 'regularly' seems to go with it; in fact 'regularly' works on 'turned' and 'out' alone scrambles the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, now mostly literary: an erstwhile colleague is a former one.

entries.clue: Youngster breaks small piece of aerial apparatus (5)

indicatorNotes.breaks: the youngster breaks into the pair of letters, splitting them apart
indicatorNotes.piece of: just the first letter of aerial

blocks.note: a cub is a young animal or junior scout

annotation.surface: A child snaps a small bit off a TV aerial.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface leads to television aerials; 'aerial apparatus' also hints at breathing air. Scuba stands for self-contained underwater breathing apparatus.
annotation.definitionFit: The acronym itself ends in 'apparatus': self-contained underwater breathing apparatus.

entries.clue: Old president, Democrat, presumably lying in the past (4)

annotation.surface: A past president, a Democrat, is suspected of having lied.
annotation.walkthrough: Lying reads as telling untruths; it means lying down. Abed is an old-fashioned word for in bed, hence 'in the past', and 'presumably' because in bed you are probably lying down.
annotation.definitionFit: Abed, an archaic word for in bed, where one is presumably lying.

entries.clue: Herald’s warning to Russell? (9)

blocks.note: Ken Russell, the British film director

annotation.surface: A herald cries a warning to someone named Russell.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue is read literally: a golfer's 'Fore!' shouted to Ken Russell, the British director of Women in Love and Tommy.
annotation.definitionFit: To foretoken is to herald, to be a sign of something to come.

entries.clue: Fan fuss following a heartless lie (10)

indicatorNotes.following: the fuss follows, coming after the rest in the answer

blocks.note: FICTION with its central T removed
ado = fuss, as in much ado

annotation.surface: A fan kicks up a fuss after being told a cruel lie.
annotation.walkthrough: Heartless looks like 'cruel' but means the middle letter goes: FICTION, a lie, loses its central T.
annotation.definitionFit: A Spanish loan word, originally for a bullfight enthusiast, now any keen fan.

entries.clue: Shared what could now be two pounds? (5-5)

blocks.note: the straight sense: split equally between two

blocks.clueFragment: what could now be two pounds?
blocks.note: read as money: two fifties, which with the pound worth half what it was could now pass for two pounds

annotation.surface: Wry comment on inflation: the pound in your pocket is worth half what it was.
annotation.walkthrough: Split equally is fifty-fifty; read as money, fifty plus fifty is a hundred pence, which the setter jokes could now be worth as much as two pounds used to be.
annotation.definitionFit: Something shared equally between two is split half and half, fifty per cent each.

entries.clue: Impracticality of documents attached to hacked emails (8)

indicatorNotes.attached to: fixed on to the front of the next piece, as a document is attached to an email
indicatorNotes.hacked: hacked emails are tampered with, so the letters are jumbled

annotation.surface: Documents attached to emails that were hacked prove impractical.
annotation.walkthrough: Documents attached to emails is an office scene; ID is the abbreviation for identity papers, and 'hacked' is a modern anagram indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: Idealism, pursuing ideals over what is achievable, can mean impracticality.

entries.clue: Property paper withdrawn, for the most part (4)

indicatorNotes.withdrawn: drawn back the way it came, so the word is written in reverse
indicatorNotes.for the most part: the greater part of the word but not all of it, so the last letter goes

annotation.surface: A property newspaper supplement has largely been pulled.
annotation.walkthrough: The paper is the Times itself; SEMIT loses its T. A semi is a semi-detached house, a common British type of property.
annotation.definitionFit: A semi is a semi-detached house, a piece of property.

entries.clue: Brief analysis raised Yorkshire river standards (8)

indicatorNotes.raised: in a down clue, lifted up, so read bottom to top

blocks.note: CRITIQUE shortened; crit is informal for a critical analysis

annotation.surface: A short report says a Yorkshire river's water standards have been raised.
annotation.walkthrough: The Aire is the river through Leeds in Yorkshire; a crit is short for critique.
annotation.definitionFit: Criteria are standards by which things are judged.

entries.clue: Check dog bite at the very least (4)

indicatorNotes.at the very least: the least possible, just the first letter

blocks.note: a cur is a mongrel dog

annotation.surface: Advice to restrain a dog, or at least stop it biting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At the very least' sounds like a hedge on the advice but keeps only the B of bite.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are verbs for holding something back; a curb was originally the chain that restrains a horse.

entries.clue: Part of game introduced by gambler’s spouse (6,4)

indicatorNotes.introduced by: the gambler comes first, introducing the part of the game

blocks.note: a football match has two halves

annotation.surface: A gambler's wife goes along to part of a match.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is not possessive: 'gambler's spouse' hides the gambler plus the link 's, with spouse the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Better half is a jokey term for one's spouse.

entries.clue: PM involved in event that’s on track (6)

blocks.note: in = involved, as in 'in on it'

annotation.surface: The Prime Minister takes part in an event that is going to plan.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On track' reads as going to plan; it is literal, a cycling track. Keirin is a paced track-cycling race, an Olympic event.
annotation.definitionFit: The keirin is a velodrome cycling race, an event on a track.

entries.clue: Lost power dividing parties in opposition with member of secret society (9)

indicatorNotes.dividing: FELL goes between the two parties
indicatorNotes.in opposition: the two DOs face each other, one written backwards

blocks.note: a government that fell lost power

annotation.surface: A deposed leader splits parties in opposition, allied with a secret-society member.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Parties in opposition' sounds political but means two parties back to back, the first reversed. The Oddfellows are a British friendly society with secret rituals.
annotation.definitionFit: An Oddfellow belongs to the Oddfellows, a fraternal society with secret rites.

entries.clue: Women’s present question (5)

blocks.note: W = women, as on toilet doors
present = here, as in a roll call

annotation.surface: A question about what present women want.
annotation.walkthrough: Present reads as a gift; it means 'here', as answered at a roll call.
annotation.definitionFit: Defined by function: an interrogative word, one of the who-what-where family used to ask questions.

entries.clue: Considerable case for theory about primitive instincts (4)

indicatorNotes.case for: the outside letters of theory, its casing
indicatorNotes.about: the case goes around the insert

blocks.note: Freud's id is the primitive, instinctive part of the mind

annotation.surface: A substantial argument for a theory about basic instincts.
annotation.walkthrough: Case reads as a legal argument; it is the outer shell of theory. A tidy sum is a considerable one.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense, mainly British: a tidy sum or tidy profit is a large one.

entries.clue: Old hat, stovepipe, finally packed away by old man (4)

indicatorNotes.finally: at the end, so only the word's final letter is used
indicatorNotes.packed away by: put inside the word that follows

annotation.surface: An old-fashioned stovepipe hat has been put away by an elderly man.
annotation.walkthrough: Stovepipe is a tall hat, so 'Old hat' looks like a description of it; it is the definition, meaning outdated.
annotation.definitionFit: Old hat means passé, and dead can mean no longer current.

entries.clue: Agent ditching lead performer (5)

blocks.note: FACTOR (an agent) without its first letter F

annotation.surface: A theatrical agent drops the star of the show.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is showbiz, with 'lead' as the star; it means the leading letter. A factor is an agent acting for someone.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a stage or screen player is one kind of performer.

entries.clue: Line of males runs through plan, failing to reach conclusion (5,4)

indicatorNotes.failing to reach conclusion: the last letter is not reached, so it is dropped

blocks.note: to run through with a weapon is to spear

annotation.surface: A plan is run through but the scheme never gets finished.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Runs through' reads as reviewing a plan; it means impales. The spear side is the male line of descent, as opposed to the distaff side.
annotation.definitionFit: A genealogical term: the spear stood for men, as the distaff for women, so descent through fathers is the male line.

entries.clue: Performing well, northern lad’s cracking try from the back (2,4)

indicatorNotes.from the back: read starting from the back end, so the word runs in reverse

blocks.note: GO (a try, an attempt) reversed, split around the insert
a son is a lad; the 's is 'is'

annotation.surface: A northern boy plays well and scores a try from the back of the field.
annotation.walkthrough: Try reads as a rugby score but means an attempt, a go. On song is British slang for in top form.
annotation.definitionFit: On song means performing at one's best.

entries.clue: Aloof, as must a bare-faced Poirot have been? (8)

annotation.definition2: as must a bare-faced Poirot have been?

blocks.note: the straight sense: standoffish, emotionally distant

blocks.clueFragment: as must a bare-faced Poirot have been?
blocks.note: Poirot is famous for his moustache; bare-faced, he has lost it

annotation.surface: Hercule Poirot without his famous moustache would look aloof.
annotation.walkthrough: Split it as DE-TACHED: tache is British slang for moustache, so a clean-shaven Poirot must have been de-tached.
annotation.definitionFit: Detached means emotionally distant, aloof.
